editorial.meta_description: The ACVS Large Animal Surgery Board Certification Exam evaluates surgical proficiency across 11 distinct domains, including musculoskeletal, gastrointestinal.
editorial.overview: The ACVS Large Animal Surgery Board Certification Exam is administered by the American College of Veterinary Surgeons. It assesses surgical knowledge and clinical competency through 11 distinct domains, ranging from musculoskeletal and gastrointestinal systems to emergency and critical care. This exam is a requirement for all veterinary professionals seeking formal board certification in large animal surgery.
editorial.who_should_take: This exam is intended for veterinary surgeons who have successfully completed an ACVS registered residency training program. Candidates must meet all credential requirements established by the American College of Veterinary Surgeons to be eligible for the examination.
editorial.preparation_strategy: Review the official reading list provided by the American College of Veterinary Surgeons. Focus on the 11 domains, prioritizing high-weight areas like musculoskeletal surgery, which accounts for 25% of the exam. Utilize the provided case-based and practical section blueprints to guide your study. Practice with sample questions to understand the format and expectations for clinical decision-making and surgical procedures. Ensure you are familiar with all technical requirements.

domain_guidance.summary: This domain focuses on the surgical management of the gastrointestinal tract in large animals, covering 16% of the total exam content. Candidates must demonstrate proficiency in intestinal function and the diagnosis and treatment of colic.

This section covers complex neurological conditions and various surgical interventions, representing 3% of the exam weight. Candidates are expected to show competency in neurological assessment and the surgical management of diverse neurological disorders in animals.

This domain addresses surgical procedures involving special senses, accounting for 3% of the exam. It requires an understanding of ocular surgery techniques and the anatomy of special senses to ensure successful clinical outcomes for patients.

This area covers respiratory system surgery and management, comprising 13% of the exam content. Candidates must be prepared to handle upper airway surgery and the management of hypoxemia to maintain patient stability during and after surgical procedures.

This domain focuses on urogenital surgical procedures, representing 9% of the exam. It covers skills related to urinary tract surgery and various reproductive system procedures, ensuring candidates can manage these systems effectively in a clinical surgical setting.

This is the largest domain, covering musculoskeletal surgery and orthopedics, accounting for 25% of the exam. Candidates must demonstrate mastery in fracture repair and joint surgery, which are components of large animal surgical practice and board certification.

This domain addresses the diagnosis and management of lameness, comprising 6% of the exam. It focuses on the systematic lameness examination process and the application of regional anesthesia to localize and treat conditions affecting the animal's movement.

This section covers cardiovascular and hemolymphatic surgical considerations, representing 3% of the exam. Candidates must understand the principles of vascular surgery and the management of the hemolymphatic system to provide care during complex surgical interventions in animals.

This domain focuses on integumentary system surgery, accounting for 6% of the exam. It emphasizes the importance of proper wound management and skin reconstruction techniques, which are vital for healing and recovery in large animal surgical patients post-operation.

This domain covers surgical preparation, instrumentation, and aseptic technique, comprising 6% of the exam. Candidates must be proficient in surgical instrument selection and the implementation of sterilization protocols to maintain a safe and effective surgical environment for patients.

This domain addresses emergency and critical care procedures, representing 9% of the exam. It covers skills in trauma management and critical care monitoring, ensuring that surgeons can respond to life-threatening situations in a clinical or surgical setting.

editorial.exam_day_guidance: Arrive at the test center prepared for a 480-minute examination. Follow all instructions provided by the ACVS regarding the case-based and practical sections. Ensure you have your registration confirmation and identification ready for check-in to facilitate a smooth and efficient start to your testing experience.

faq.answer_text: The ACVS Large Animal Surgery Board Certification Exam is an assessment that has a total duration of 480 minutes, requiring candidates to manage their time effectively across all sections to complete the requirements.

faq.question_title: What domains are covered on the exam?
faq.answer_text: The exam covers 11 distinct domains, including gastrointestinal, neurological, special senses, respiratory, urogenital, musculoskeletal, lameness, cardiovascular, integumentary, surgical preparation, and emergency care, ensuring a broad evaluation of surgical expertise for all candidates.

faq.question_title: What is the weight of the musculoskeletal domain?
faq.answer_text: The musculoskeletal domain is the largest and most significant section of the exam, accounting for 25% of the total weight, reflecting its importance in the field of large animal surgery and board certification.

faq.question_title: Where can I find information on the current certification path?
faq.answer_text: For detailed information regarding the long-term certification path and all associated requirements, please check with the American College of Veterinary Surgeons (ACVS) for the current certification path to ensure you have the most accurate guidance.
